title: Resist the beginnings (I.13)
hookLine: temptations are easiest to overcome at the start
tomorrow: so why put up with someone's worst habit?

lines: WHERE COULD IT HAVE BEEN STOPPED?
cards: A phone glows on a nightstand at 11:52. A stranger's post, and one thought knocks: what an idiot. A minute later the thought has a picture, the perfect reply, sharp enough to sting.
Then it starts to feel good, warm, almost fun. Thumbs moving now. Three sentences.
A fourth. Nobody decided any of this. It walked in one step at a time, and now it's sitting at the kitchen table with its shoes off.
So where, exactly, could it have been stopped?

teach.h: THE LIFE OF MAN IS A WARFARE.
teach.b: The Imitation's answer: at the door. Chapter thirteen of book one starts honestly.
As long as we live, it says, trouble and temptation come with life, and it leans on Job, in the Douay-Rheims: "The life of man upon earth is a warfare."
No religious order so holy, no place so hidden, that temptation can't reach it. Then comes the map, the part worth keeping.
First a plain thought comes to mind. Then a strong picture. Then delight.
Then a wrong movement. Then consent. At each step the enemy gets further in, because he wasn't met at the start.
It's an honest little map of the inside of a person.

So watch most at the beginning, the book says: an enemy is beaten more easily if he's never let through the door of the mind, but met outside the moment he knocks. Here's one to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: A LINE FROM A LOVE POET.
teach.b: To make the point, this book of devotion borrows a line from a Roman poet.

Principiis obsta, resist the beginnings, comes from Ovid's Remedies for Love, advice for getting over someone. A monk's handbook and a love poet agree: once the trouble has grown strong, the cure comes late.
And the chapter isn't grim. Temptations, it says, can humble a person, cleanse them and teach them. Nobody is expected to never hear a knock.

how: Catholics speak of avoiding the 'near occasion of sin' and of turning to prayer at the first sign of temptation; the Imitation's chapter on resisting temptation is a common source for that teaching in spiritual reading.

o: fight temptation hardest once it's at full strength
meet temptation early, while it's only a thought
never start anything new without a careful plan

games.q: you promised yourself no phone after 11. it's 11:05 and a thought shows up: just check one thing. by the Imitation's map, when's the easiest moment to say no?
o: right now, while it's only a thought.
after one quick look, once you know what's there.
once you're scrolling and it's clearly a problem.
games.why: the chapter says the enemy is beaten more easily at the door. every step after the thought, the picture, the delight, makes it stronger.

practice: Sit still and let your mind run for a moment. When a pull shows up, a craving, a grudge, the itch to check your phone, catch it at the first step, while it's only a thought, and let it knock without opening.
If you pray, you can turn to God right there at the threshold.

wordCard.voice: Resist the beginnings. The Imitation's counsel for temptation: meet it at the door, while it's still only a thought.

orig.note: Latin: resist the beginnings; Ovid's line, which the Imitation quotes in its chapter on temptation.

carryVoice: The line to keep: at the start, when it's still a knock and not a guest. Good night.
